category: anonymous transfer.sh-shaped upload (PUT a body, get a JSON link)

free_tier.stated: 3-day expiry and a JSON link from a single PUT, no account. The site advertises 'a retention period that depends on file size' and the upload reply carried expiresAt three days out.
free_tier.notes: The upload host is ul.sto.care and the download host is trystocare.com; the brand and both domains disagree.

per_object_cap.stated: unverified: no size cap is stated on the pages read; 1 MiB was accepted
per_object_cap.notes: A 100 MB cap is mentioned by a third-party blog for a different product on the same site, so it was not carried over.

retention.stated: expiresAt 2026-10-26T02:22:40.454Z for an upload at 2026-10-23T02:22:40Z, so 72 hours
retention.notes: Measured from the reply field, not from the page.

egress.terms: Downloads are served from trystocare.com. The site advertises a 10-download limit per link, which makes the link a distribution budget rather than a store.

interface_detail: curl -T file https://ul.sto.care/<name> returns JSON {url, expiresAt}, with the download URL on a different host.
tooling: Any HTTP client that can PUT a file; the transfer.sh one-liner works with the hostname swapped
chaining: A transfer.sh-shaped PUT is the cheapest thing to wire into a script that already speaks that idiom, and the JSON reply makes the link parseable, but 3 days and a per-link download count make it a hand-off, not a mirror.

limits.source: measured: expiresAt in the upload reply

limits_note: The download limit was not exercised: 10 fetches of one link would settle it, and the second fetch is the interesting one because the first may not count.
binding_note: At 1 TiB a month no published byte cap was hit, but a 10-download link means a re-fetch of the same object fails once ten readers have had it, and 72 hours bounds it again; the pull count is the first of the two that a busy object meets.

identity_cost.detail: A bare PUT with no cookie, no account and no email returned a link.

reliability_note: The upload host and the download host are different domains, so a client that allow-lists the upload domain breaks at retrieval.
confidence_note: Upload and read-back at 1 MiB with a matching SHA-256; the cap and the 10-download limit are vendor claims and were not pushed.

evidence.proved: read-back 1 048 576 bytes, sha256 da0099c231f1182a5d411c8ac5149dfb7a2e3578a3970928490cb78ba92aecc9, full-body hash matched
'You get a JSON link that allows 10 downloads over 72 hours' - the vendor's own blog, which is the only place either number is stated
the service positions itself as a 0x0.st and transfer.sh replacement with a curl one-liner

notes: A credible transfer.sh replacement that actually answers, and the only measured relay that returns a machine-readable expiry. The caveat is that its own documentation lives in blog posts rather than a docs page.
